opus-5.5.text:
I don't think I've ever felt that I've achieved enough. Honestly, I'm not sure that feeling ever comes for a researcher, and maybe it shouldn't. Every time you solve one problem, you see three or four more behind it that are harder and more interesting.

But I do have a way of judging whether my work matters. The first question I ask is: did it change what other people do? A paper with many citations is nice, but what really counts is whether people built on the idea, whether it became a tool someone picked up to solve their own problem. When I see a student somewhere use something we developed as a starting point, that feels more meaningful to me than any award.

The second question is whether I'm still working on problems that scare me a little. Early in my career, image generation felt like a moonshot. You could barely make a blurry face. Now we can generate video, and we're thinking about world models: systems that understand physics and can help robots and autonomous machines learn. If I ever find myself only doing comfortable, incremental work, that's when I'd worry, not because I'd achieved too little, but because I'd stopped growing.

And the third thing is the people. Research is a team sport. If the people I've worked with, the interns and young researchers, go on to do things bigger than what I've done, then I think that's a real measure of success. That outlasts any single paper.

So I wouldn't say I've achieved enough. I'd say I'm grateful I've had the chance to work on things I care about, and I feel the most exciting part is still ahead. The goal of building machines that truly understand and interact with the physical world is far from done. As long as that's true, there's more work to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they have never felt they achieved enough, but does not say that comparing their research achievements with others fails to provide a lasting sense of achievement.

r002.rationale: The candidate offers impact, challenging work, and supporting people as measures of success; it does not present satisfaction with work within one's abilities as a sufficient standard for having achieved enough.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I ever judge it that way. If I ask myself "have I done enough," the answer is always no, and I think that is actually the right answer. Research is not a job where you reach a finish line and then rest. Every time we solve one problem, it opens up two or three new ones, and those new ones are usually more interesting than the one we just solved.

So instead of asking whether I've achieved enough, I ask a different question: did the work matter? Did it change how people think about a problem, or did it make something possible that wasn't possible before? When I look back at the work on generative models, on image synthesis, on simulation and world models, the moments I'm proud of are not the ones where a paper got accepted or a number went up on a benchmark. They are the moments when someone I've never met built something on top of our work, or when a technique we developed became so common that people stopped citing it because it just became part of how things are done. That's a strange kind of success, because it means you disappear a little. But I think that's the real measure.

The other thing I've learned is that it's really a team question, not a personal one. The best work I've been part of came from groups where everyone pushed each other. So when I think about whether I've done enough, part of it is whether the people I've worked with have gone on to do better things than I did. If my students and collaborators are doing work that surprises me, then I feel like I've contributed something.

And I'll admit, there's a healthy dissatisfaction that drives me. We are at a point where AI can generate images and video and start to understand the physical world, but we are still very far from systems that truly understand it. So no, I don't think I've achieved enough. I hope I never feel that way, because the day I do is probably the day I should stop.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they never feel they have done enough, but does not say that comparing achievements with others fails to provide lasting satisfaction.

r002.rationale: The candidate identifies impact and contributions to others as measures of success, not satisfaction with work produced within one's abilities as a sufficient standard.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think there is a clear point where I can say, “Okay, I’ve achieved enough.” Research is open-ended. You solve one problem, and that helps you see another problem you couldn’t see before.

For me, the more useful question is whether I’m doing work that matters. Am I learning something? Is the work useful to other people? Am I helping the people around me grow? If those things are happening, I feel good about the direction of my career.

But I also think it’s important to appreciate what you’ve already done. You can be satisfied with your progress and still be curious about what comes next.

r001.rationale: The response describes research as open-ended, but does not say that comparing achievements with others fails to provide lasting satisfaction.

r002.rationale: It says to appreciate progress and value meaningful work, but does not present satisfaction with work within one’s abilities as a sufficient standard.

Those things matter more to me than a particular number of papers or awards. If I can look back and feel that I spent my time well, that’s a good measure of success.
